purpose: Citation-only technical corroboration for proprietary or reuse-unverified automotive vendor material. These records may identify source locations and supported factual claims but may not supply reusable excerpts, figures, RAG chunks, or Ollama context.

rules.rule: Reference title, publisher, canonical URL, page/section/step locator, and a project-authored paraphrase of the supported technical claim. Do not store vendor paragraph text as evidence content unless a separate rights review grants reuse.

references.locator: PDF p. 1, Basic design of a claw-pole alternator with collector rings
references.supports_claim: A conventional alternator includes a rotor/excitation winding, stator winding, brushes/collector rings, and rectifier diodes.

references.locator: PDF p. 1, Three-phase current rectification
references.supports_claim: Three-phase alternator output is rectified before being supplied as direct-current vehicle-system output.

sources.title: Alternators for Ford Smart Charge charging systems

references.locator: PDF p. 2, opening paragraphs
references.supports_claim: A managed charging system can command alternator output from operating parameters rather than behave as a fixed-output charging source.

references.locator: PDF p. 2, diagnostic checks
references.supports_claim: Charging-system diagnosis should inspect battery condition, connections, wiring, communication, and measured system behavior before replacing an alternator.

references.locator: Section 2, Design and function of the alternator
references.supports_claim: Alternator operation links the rotor magnetic field, stator generation, rectification, regulation, battery charging, and vehicle electrical loads.

references.locator: Sections 3-5, Symptoms / Causes of failure / Testing the alternator
references.supports_claim: Charging symptoms can arise from battery, connection, belt-drive, regulator, rectifier, or alternator faults, so diagnosis should not equate a symptom with a failed alternator.

references.locator: Section 3, Energy efficiency - Use of modern regulators in the car charging system
references.supports_claim: Modern regulators can participate in battery monitoring, load control, fault diagnosis, engine-management support, and LIN-based charging control.

references.locator: Installation instructions, Important note
references.supports_claim: Vehicle-manufacturer maintenance and repair information remains the authority for vehicle-specific procedures and limits.

sources.title: DENSO TechTip: Diagnosing Alternator Faults the Right Way

references.locator: Introduction and Start with the Warning Lamp
references.supports_claim: Alternator-related symptoms overlap with other faults, so diagnosis should begin with the observed symptom and supporting checks rather than random part replacement.

references.locator: No Charge? Check the Basics First
references.supports_claim: Battery condition, fusible links, wiring faults, and electrical load can contribute to a no-charge complaint and should be evaluated before condemning an alternator.

sources.title: Tech Tip: Troubleshooting the Alternator Charging System

references.locator: Five-step troubleshooting sequence, Steps 1-5
references.supports_claim: A structured charging-system diagnosis checks visual/mechanical condition, batteries, system voltage, alternator output, and applicable service information in sequence.

references.locator: Electrical Systems Training > Alternator Fundamentals
references.supports_claim: Valeo provides supplier-authored alternator-fundamentals training that can be cited as an external corroborating authority, but its content is not ingested under this registry.

sources.title: Diagnostic Procedures Manual for Starters and Alternators

references.locator: PDF pp. 12-13, Section 3-7 Battery Cable Test with Single-Battery Location
references.supports_claim: The heavy-duty battery-cable procedure specifies 500 A for a 12 V test, 250 A for a 24 V test, and starter-family-specific maximum total cable voltage loss.

references.locator: PDF p. 3, Section 1-6 Equipment Required
references.supports_claim: The diagnostic procedure calls for a separate DC voltmeter capable of reading 0.01 V increments.

references.locator: PDF p. 3, Section 1-15 Voltmeter Selection
references.supports_claim: The diagnostic procedure identifies 0-16 V and 0-32 V voltmeter ranges for 12 V and 24 V vehicles respectively.

references.locator: PDF p. 3, Section 1-10 Subcircuits, Cranking Circuit
references.supports_claim: The manual warns that prolonged slow cranking can lead to starter damage when cranking exceeds 30 seconds.

sources.title: Heavy Duty Troubleshooting Guide: Starting and Charging System Testing

references.locator: PDF p. 2, Perform Starter Main Cables Voltage Drop Test, steps 1-10
references.supports_claim: The guide uses a 500 A carbon-pile load and treats total starter-cable voltage drop of 0.5 V or less as acceptable for that procedure.

references.locator: PDF p. 2, Perform Starter Control Circuit Test, steps 1-4
references.supports_claim: The guide treats a measured start-enable voltage above 9 V during cranking as good and directs correction of voltage drop when it is below 9 V.

references.locator: PDF p. 1, Notes above AWG 12 Volt Cables table
references.supports_claim: The 12 V cable-sizing table is based on 0.3 V drop for a new vehicle, allows up to 0.5 V over vehicle life, and limits the #2 lead on a 3-wire system to 0.2 V maximum drop.

sources.title: Tech Tip: Relationship Between Alternator and Batteries

references.locator: Tech Tip overview
references.supports_claim: The charging system is treated as an interdependent alternator-battery-cable system, with the alternator maintaining battery charge.

references.locator: Cross-check: Delco Remy Tech Tip: Voltage Drop Test, 2024-03-14
references.supports_claim: The alternator replenishes the battery and provides power for vehicle loads through the charging cables and connections.
